newsitem.title: USA: NY Gov calls for ending estate, gift taxes.
newsitem.headline: NY Gov calls for ending estate, gift taxes.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki, who has made big tax cuts a centerpiece of his Administration's efforts to make the state more competitive, on Thursday proposed eliminating estate and gift taxes.

Pataki, who estimated that eliminating the two taxes by 1999 would save New Yorkers almost $400 million, said his plan will protect families, seniors, family farmers and small business owners, who no longer will see their estates or their gifts to children taxed, and thus have less incentive to leave the state.

"Middle-class and working families need every advantage that we can give them as they build a better life for themselves and their children," he said in prepared remarks. "This tax cut will encourage New Yorkers to stay home and build a better life here for themselves and their children."

New York residents now face the highest estate taxes in the nation, paying from two to 21 percent, and Pataki pointed out that the former Cuomo Administration started taxing all estates valued at more than $115,000.

Pataki's new plan would raise the state exemption to the federal level of $600,000, aiding 85 percent of residents who file estate taxes, while wealthier individuals would see taxes on their estates fall on a sliding scale to about 25 percent. The changes would be fully implemented by July 1, 1999.

Gift taxes, which first were levied in 1972, would be repaled by Jan 1, 1999, said Pataki, noting the New York was one of only six states that imposed such taxes. The tax now limits transfers to $10,000 per individual, double the amount for a couple, in any one year, and a total of $115,000 can be exempted over an individual's life.
